tasks.title: Security Hardening: Remove Exposed Credentials and Secure Environment
tasks.description: Remove the exposed GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) from the codebase and ensure the .env file is properly ignored by version control to prevent future credential leaks.
tasks.details: 1. Locate the .env file containing the exposed GitHub PAT. 2. Remove the PAT from the file. If it's needed for a dependency, source it from a secure environment variable provider or a secure secret management system. 3. Ensure the `.gitignore` file at the root of the project contains a line for `.env` and `*.env`. 4. Verify that no history of the .env file exists in the Git repository. If it does, the history must be rewritten using tools like `git filter-repo` or BFG Repo-Cleaner to completely remove the sensitive data. 5. Rotate the leaked PAT on GitHub immediately.
tasks.testStrategy: 1. Run `git check-ignore .env` to confirm the file is ignored. 2. Clone the repository in a fresh directory and verify the .env file is not present. 3. Search the Git history using `git log -S'GITHUB_PAT'` to ensure the token is no longer present in historical commits.

subtasks.title: Immediately Rotate Exposed GitHub PAT
subtasks.description: The first and most critical step is to invalidate the leaked Personal Access Token on GitHub to prevent unauthorized access. A new token should be generated if it is still required for any services.
subtasks.details:
Log into the GitHub account associated with the leaked PAT. Navigate to Settings -> Developer settings -> Personal access tokens. Find the compromised token, revoke it, and delete it. If the token is necessary for CI/CD, generate a new one with minimal permissions and store it as a secure secret.

</info added on 2025-11-26T16:43:31.211Z>
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that any scripts or services using the old token fail to authenticate after it has been revoked. Confirm the new token (if created) works correctly in its intended environment (e.g., GitHub Actions).

subtasks.title: Remove .env File from Git Tracking
subtasks.description: Remove the `.env` file from the Git index to ensure it is no longer tracked by version control, without deleting the local file itself.
subtasks.details: First, locate the `.env` file in the project root and delete the line containing the `GITHUB_PAT`. Then, run the command `git rm --cached .env` to untrack the file. This will stage the deletion of the file from the repository index for the next commit.
subtasks.testStrategy: After running the command, execute `git status`. The output should show the `.env` file as 'deleted' in the staging area. The local `.env` file should still exist in the filesystem.

subtasks.title: Update .gitignore to Exclude Environment Files
subtasks.description: Add entries for `.env` and similar configuration files to the project's root `.gitignore` file to prevent them from being accidentally committed in the future.
subtasks.details:
Open the `.gitignore` file at the root of the project. Add the following lines if they are not already present: `
.env
*.env`. This pattern will ignore the main `.env` file and any variants like `.env.local` or `.env.production`. Commit this change along with the untracked file from the previous step.
subtasks.testStrategy: From the project root, run the command `git check-ignore .env`. The command should output `.env`, confirming that Git is now correctly ignoring the file. Attempting to stage the file with `git add --force .env` should work, but a normal `git add .env` should not.

subtasks.title: Scan Git History for Leaked Credentials
subtasks.description: Thoroughly scan the entire Git commit history to determine if the Personal Access Token or the `.env` file was ever committed. This is crucial for identifying the full extent of the leak.
subtasks.details:
Use Git commands to search the repository's history. Run `git log -S "<PASTE_THE_LEAKED_TOKEN_HERE>"` to find commits that introduced or removed the specific token value. Also, run `git log --all --full-history -- "**/.env"` to find any commits that affected an `.env` file. Document any commit hashes found.
<info added on 2025-11-26T16:56:37.494Z>
The scan of the entire Git history is complete. Results confirm that no sensitive data, including the .env file, GitHub PAT, or Gemini API Key, was ever committed. The repository history is clean, making Task 1.5 (Purge Sensitive Data from Git History) unnecessary.
</info added on 2025-11-26T16:56:37.494Z>
subtasks.testStrategy: The successful execution of the search commands is the test. If the commands return any commit hashes, the scan has successfully identified historical leaks. If no commits are found, the history is clean and the next subtask can be skipped.

subtasks.title: Purge Sensitive Data from Git History
subtasks.description: If the previous scan revealed the PAT in the commit history, the history must be rewritten to permanently remove the sensitive data. This is a destructive operation and requires coordination with the entire team.
subtasks.details: This task is conditional on the outcome of subtask 4. If credentials were found, use a tool like `git-filter-repo` to remove the specific file (`.env`) or the string value of the PAT from all historical commits. This action will rewrite commit hashes and requires a force push (`git push --force`) to the remote repository. All collaborators must be notified as they will need to re-clone or carefully reset their local branches.
subtasks.testStrategy: After rewriting history and force-pushing, clone the repository into a new, clean directory. Run the same search commands from subtask 4 (`git log -S "..."`). The commands must now return no results, confirming the sensitive data has been successfully purged from the entire history.

tasks.title: Implement Firestore Security Rules
tasks.description: Define and apply Firestore security rules for the users, vehicles, and consultation_requests collections to enforce proper access control and data validation.
tasks.details:
Develop and deploy `firestore.rules`. The rules should enforce that: 
- `users`: A user can only read/write their own document (`allow read, write: if request.auth.uid == userId;`). Publicly readable fields should be explicitly allowed. 
- `vehicles`: Any authenticated user can read vehicle documents. Only authorized admins or the vehicle owner (if allowed) can create/update/delete. Writes should validate data types (e.g., `price` is a number). 
- `consultation_requests`: Users can only create requests for themselves. They can only read their own requests. Admins should have read/write access to all requests. 
- `Firebase Storage`: Rules for image uploads should ensure that only authenticated users can upload images and that file size and type are validated.
tasks.testStrategy: 1. Use the Firebase Emulator Suite to test rules locally. 2. Write unit tests for security rules using the `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` library. 3. Create test cases for authenticated users, unauthenticated users, and admins attempting valid and invalid read/write operations on each collection.

subtasks.title: Initialize Firestore and Storage Rules Files and Configure Emulator
subtasks.description: Create the `firestore.rules` and `storage.rules` files. Set up the basic rules structure with a default deny-all policy. Configure the Firebase Emulator Suite for local testing of these rules.
subtasks.details:
Create `firestore.rules` and `storage.rules` in the project root. In `firestore.rules`, add `rules_version = '2'; service cloud.firestore { match /databases/{database}/documents { match /{document=**} { allow read, write: if false; } } }`. A similar deny-all rule should be added to `storage.rules`. This establishes a secure baseline before adding specific permissions.

subtasks.details:
In `firestore.rules`, add a match block for `/users/{userId}`. Implement the rule `allow read, write: if request.auth.uid == userId;`. Also, create a global helper function `isAdmin()` which checks if the requesting user has an `isAdmin: true` field in their own user document: `get(/databases/$(database)/documents/users/$(request.auth.uid)).data.isAdmin == true`.
<info added on 2025-11-27T01:01:51.019Z>
The implementation in `firestore.rules` for the `/users/{userId}` path is complete. The `isAdmin()` helper function was created to check if the requesting user's document contains `role == 'admin'`. The final rules allow a user to read and write their own document, but also grant read access to any user document for users with the 'admin' role. The logic is effectively `allow read: if request.auth.uid == userId || isAdmin();` and `allow write: if request.auth.uid == userId;`.
</info added on 2025-11-27T01:01:51.019Z>

subtasks.details:

Add data validation to ensure incoming data (`request.resource.data`) contains required fields and that `price` and `year` are numbers.

subtasks.title: Implement Security Rules for the 'consultation_requests' Collection
subtasks.description: Define security rules for the `consultation_requests` collection. Users must only be able to create requests for themselves and read their own requests. Admins require full read/write access to all requests.
subtasks.details:
Add a match block for `/consultation_requests/{requestId}`. The `read` rule should be `allow read: if request.auth.uid == resource.data.userId || isAdmin();`. The `create` rule should be `allow create: if request.auth.uid == request.resource.data.userId;`. The `update` and `delete` rules should be `allow update, delete: if isAdmin();`.

Add the following properties: `JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE=path/to/your/jcar-upload-key.keystore`, `JCAR_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS=jcar_upload_alias`, `JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD=your_store_password`, and `JCAR_UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD=your_key_password`. Ensure that `gradle.properties` is included in the root `.gitignore` file to prevent it from being committed.
subtasks.testStrategy: Run `git check-ignore android/gradle.properties` to confirm the file is ignored by Git. Verify that Gradle can read these properties by adding a `println` statement in `build.gradle` and running a sync.

subtasks.title: Configure Release Signing in build.gradle
subtasks.description: Modify the `android/app/build.gradle` file to read the secure credentials from `gradle.properties` and apply the signing configuration to the `release` build type.
subtasks.details: In `android/app/build.gradle`, define a `signingConfigs` block for `release` that reads the properties set in the previous task. The configuration should look like: `storeFile file(JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE)`, `storePassword JCAR_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD`, etc. Then, within the `buildTypes.release` block, set `signingConfig signingConfigs.release`.
subtasks.testStrategy: From the `android` directory, run the `./gradlew :app:signingReport` command. Check the output to ensure the 'release' variant is correctly configured with the 'jcar_upload_alias' and shows no errors.

subtasks.title: Enable Code Shrinking and Obfuscation with R8
subtasks.description: Enable R8 for the release build to reduce app size, remove unused code, and obfuscate class and method names, which enhances security.
subtasks.details: In the `release` build type within `android/app/build.gradle`, set `minifyEnabled true` and `shrinkResources true`. Check for any third-party libraries that might require specific rules to function correctly after minification. Add any necessary `-keep` rules to the `android/app/proguard-rules.pro` file to prevent critical code from being stripped.
subtasks.testStrategy: After generating a release AAB, analyze it using Android Studio's 'Analyze APK' tool to inspect the dex files and confirm that code has been obfuscated. The primary test is to install and run the app to ensure no crashes occur due to incorrect ProGuard rules.

subtasks.title: Generate and Verify Signed Android App Bundle (AAB)
subtasks.description: Execute the final Gradle command to build the signed Android App Bundle (AAB) and perform a verification test on a physical device to ensure its integrity and functionality.
subtasks.details: Navigate to the `android` directory in your terminal and run the command `./gradlew bundleRelease`. This command will compile the code, run R8, and sign the application, producing the final AAB file located at `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Install the generated `app-release.aab` on a physical Android device, either via `bundletool` or by uploading it to an internal testing track on the Google Play Console. Perform a full smoke test of the application's core features, such as login, vehicle browsing, and consultation requests.

tasks.title: Establish Design System Foundation (Theme)
tasks.description: Create the core theme files for the design system, including color palettes, typography, spacing, border radius, and shadow styles. This will serve as the single source of truth for all UI styling.
tasks.details: Create a `src/theme` directory. Inside, create separate files for each design token category: `colors.js`, `typography.js`, `spacing.js`, `shadows.js`, `borderRadius.js`. Export constants from each file. For example, in `colors.js`: `export const colors = { primary: '#2B4593', success: '#28A745', ... }`. Create a main `index.js` in `src/theme` that exports all tokens as a single theme object. Use React's Context API to provide this theme object to the entire application tree via a `ThemeProvider` component.
tasks.testStrategy: Unit test the theme files to ensure all values from the PRD are correctly defined and exported. Manually review the theme object structure. Integrate the ThemeProvider at the root of the app and verify in a sample component that theme values can be accessed correctly.

subtasks.title: Set Up Theme Directory and File Structure
subtasks.description: Create the necessary directory and empty files for the design system's theme foundation.
subtasks.details: Create a new directory at `src/theme`. Inside this directory, create the following empty files: `colors.js`, `typography.js`, `spacing.js`, `shadows.js`, `borderRadius.js`, and a main `index.js` file for consolidation.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the `src/theme` directory and all specified `.js` files exist in the project structure.

subtasks.title: Define and Export Individual Design Tokens
subtasks.description: Populate each theme file with the specific design tokens (colors, typography, etc.) and export them as constants.
subtasks.details: In each file created in the previous step, define and export the corresponding design tokens. For example, in `src/theme/colors.js`, add `export const colors = { primary: '#2B4593', secondary: '#...', ... }`. Do this for all token files based on the project's PRD.
subtasks.testStrategy: Unit test each file to ensure that it exports a non-empty object with the correct structure and that the values match the design specifications.

subtasks.title: Consolidate All Tokens into a Single Theme Object
subtasks.description: Import all individual token objects into the main theme index file and export them as a single, unified theme object.
subtasks.details: In `src/theme/index.js`, import the constants from `colors.js`, `typography.js`, `spacing.js`, etc. Combine them into a single `theme` object and export it as the default export. Example: `export default { colors, typography, ... }`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Create a test that imports the default export from `src/theme/index.js` and verifies that it is an object containing all the individual token categories as properties (e.g., `theme.colors`, `theme.typography`).

subtasks.title: Create ThemeProvider using React Context API
subtasks.description: Develop a ThemeProvider component that uses React's Context API to make the theme object available to all descendant components.
subtasks.details: Create a new file, for example `src/providers/ThemeProvider.js`. In this file, create a `ThemeContext`. Then, create a `ThemeProvider` component that accepts `children` and provides the consolidated theme object (imported from `src/theme`) through the `ThemeContext.Provider`. Also, create and export a custom hook `useTheme` for easy consumption of the context.
subtasks.testStrategy: Unit test the `ThemeProvider` to ensure it renders its children. Test the `useTheme` hook within a test component wrapped by the provider to verify it returns the correct theme object.

subtasks.title: Integrate ThemeProvider at the Application Root
subtasks.description: Wrap the root component of the application with the new ThemeProvider to make the theme available globally.
subtasks.details: Locate the main entry point of the application (e.g., `App.js`). Import the `ThemeProvider` and wrap the entire application's component tree with it. This will ensure that any component can access the theme via the `useTheme` hook.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually test the application after integration. Modify a sample component to use the `useTheme` hook and apply a theme style (e.g., `color: theme.colors.primary`). Verify that the style is correctly applied when the app runs.

tasks.title: Develop Unified Button Component
tasks.description: Create a single, reusable Button component that supports all variants (Primary, Secondary, Danger, Success, Text) and states (Default, Hover, Pressed, Disabled) defined in the PRD.
tasks.details: Create a `src/components/Button.js` file. The component should accept props like `variant`, `onPress`, `disabled`, and `title`. Use the theme values from the context for styling. Implement dynamic styling based on the `variant` prop. For example: `const getBackgroundColor = () => { switch(variant) { case 'primary': return theme.colors.primary; case 'danger': return theme.colors.danger; default: return 'transparent'; } };`. Use `Pressable` to handle states like `onPressIn` and `onPressOut` to apply pressed styles (scale transform).
tasks.testStrategy: Use Storybook or a similar tool to visually test all variants and states. Write unit tests using React Native Testing Library to verify that the correct styles are applied for each prop combination and that the `onPress` handler is called when not disabled, and not called when disabled.

subtasks.title: Create Button.js File and Basic Component Structure
subtasks.description: Set up the initial `Button.js` file with a basic functional component structure. It should accept `title` and `onPress` props and render a `Pressable` component containing a `Text` component for the title.
subtasks.details: Create the file `src/components/Button.js`. The component will accept props `(title, onPress, ...rest)`. It will return a `<Pressable onPress={onPress}><Text>{title}</Text></Pressable>`. Apply initial, default styling for the container and text.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually render the component on a development screen to ensure it displays correctly with a title and is clickable.

subtasks.title: Implement Dynamic Styles for All Button Variants
subtasks.description: Implement the styling logic to support all five variants: Primary, Secondary, Danger, Success, and Text. Styles should be derived from the application's theme context.
subtasks.details: Import and use the application's theme context (e.g., via a `useTheme` hook). Create a style generation function or use a `switch` statement that returns an object with `backgroundColor`, `borderColor`, and `textColor` based on the `variant` prop. Apply these styles to the `Pressable` and `Text` elements.
subtasks.testStrategy: Write a unit test that provides each variant prop to the component and asserts that the returned style object contains the correct theme colors. Visually confirm each variant in the app.

subtasks.title: Implement Styling and Logic for Pressed and Disabled States
subtasks.description: Add visual feedback for the `pressed` state and functional/visual changes for the `disabled` state. The button should provide interaction feedback and appear inactive when disabled.
subtasks.details: Use the `Pressable` component's function-as-a-child for the `style` prop: `style={({ pressed }) => [...]}`. When `pressed`, apply a transform style, e.g., `transform: [{ scale: 0.98 }]`. When the `disabled` prop is true, merge an opacity style (e.g., `{ opacity: 0.5 }`) and ensure the `onPress` handler is blocked.
subtasks.testStrategy: Using React Native Testing Library, simulate a press event and verify the `onPress` callback is not fired when `disabled` is true. Manually press the button to confirm the visual transform and check the disabled appearance.

subtasks.title: Define Prop Types and Finalize Component API
subtasks.description: Formalize the component's public API by adding PropType definitions or TypeScript types for all accepted props, including setting default values.
subtasks.details: Import `PropTypes` from 'prop-types'. Define `Button.propTypes` specifying the type for each prop: `variant` as `oneOf(['primary', 'secondary', 'danger', 'success', 'text'])`, `title` as `string.isRequired`, `onPress` as `func.isRequired`, `disabled` as `bool`. Set default props, e.g., `Button.defaultProps = { variant: 'primary', disabled: false };`.
subtasks.testStrategy: This is a static code quality task. The test is to run the application's linter or type-checker to ensure the definitions are correct and that console warnings are not thrown for valid prop usage.

subtasks.title: Create Storybook for Visual Testing and Documentation
subtasks.description: Develop a Storybook story file for the Button component to visually test all variants and states in an isolated environment, which will also serve as living documentation.
subtasks.details: Create a new file `src/components/Button.stories.js`. Write stories for each `variant`. For each variant, display its default, pressed (via addon), and disabled states to ensure all visual combinations render as expected.
subtasks.testStrategy: The successful creation and rendering of the Storybook stories is the test. Manually navigate through each story in the Storybook UI to visually confirm that all variants and states match the design specifications from the PRD.

tasks.title: Develop Unified Input Field Component
tasks.description: Create a reusable text input component with consistent styling for default, focus, and error states as specified in the PRD.
tasks.details: Create `src/components/InputField.js`. This component will wrap React Native's `TextInput`. It should accept props like `value`, `onChangeText`, `placeholder`, `error` (a string for the error message), etc. Use the `useState` hook to track focus state (`onFocus`, `onBlur`). Apply conditional styling based on focus and the presence of the `error` prop. The error message should be displayed below the input field using the 'Danger' color. All styling (height, padding, border radius, colors) should come from the theme.
tasks.testStrategy: Visually test the component in different states: default, focused, with input text, and with an error message. Write unit tests to check that the border color and style change on focus/blur, and that the error message is rendered correctly when the `error` prop is provided.

subtasks.title: Create Basic InputField Component Structure
subtasks.description: Create the file `src/components/InputField.js` and set up a basic functional component that wraps the React Native `TextInput`. The component should accept and pass through essential props like `value`, `onChangeText`, and `placeholder`.
subtasks.details: Initialize the file at `src/components/InputField.js`. The component should return a `View` containing a `TextInput`. Ensure props like `value`, `onChangeText`, and `placeholder` are correctly passed to the `TextInput` element.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that the component renders a text input and that typing in it works as expected.

subtasks.title: Apply Default Styles from Theme
subtasks.description: Integrate the application's theme to apply default styling to the InputField. This includes border radius, background color, padding, text color, and border color for the default (non-focused, no-error) state.
subtasks.details: Use the theme context to access style values. Create a StyleSheet for the component. Apply theme values for `colors.border`, `colors.text`, `spacing.padding`, `borderRadius`, and a fixed height as specified in the PRD.
subtasks.testStrategy: Visually inspect the component to ensure it matches the default state styling defined in the design specifications. Check that all style values are derived from the theme.

subtasks.title: Implement Focus State and Styling
subtasks.description: Use the `useState` hook to track the input's focus state. Implement `onFocus` and `onBlur` handlers to update the state, and apply conditional styling when the input is focused, such as changing the border color.
subtasks.details: Create a state variable `isFocused` initialized to `false`. The `onFocus` prop of `TextInput` should set `isFocused` to `true`, and `onBlur` should set it to `false`. Use this state to conditionally change the `borderColor` to `theme.colors.primary`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Manually test by tapping in and out of the input field. Verify that the border color changes to the primary theme color on focus and reverts to the default color on blur.

subtasks.title: Implement Error State and Message Display
subtasks.description: Handle the `error` prop. When an error string is passed, the input's border color should change to the 'danger' color. The error message itself should be displayed in a `Text` component directly below the input field.
subtasks.details: The component should accept an `error` prop (string). If `error` has a value, override other border color styles with `theme.colors.danger`. Render a `<Text>` component conditionally (`{error && <Text>...}`), styling it with `theme.colors.danger`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Pass a sample error string to the `error` prop and verify that the border becomes red and the error message appears below the input in the correct color.

subtasks.title: Finalize Props and Add Documentation
subtasks.description: Ensure any additional `TextInput` props can be passed to the underlying component using the `...rest` spread operator. Add comprehensive JSDoc comments or PropTypes to document the component's API.
subtasks.details: Modify the component's props to include `{ ...rest }`. Pass this `rest` object directly to the `TextInput` component. Add documentation for primary props like `value`, `onChangeText`, `placeholder`, and `error`.
subtasks.testStrategy: Test passing a standard `TextInput` prop like `keyboardType='numeric'` or `secureTextEntry` to the `InputField` component and verify it functions correctly.

tasks.title: Develop Card and Status Badge Components
tasks.description: Create reusable Card and Badge components. The Card will be a container for content sections, and the Badge will be used to display status labels like '대기중', '승인', etc.

For `src/components/Badge.js`, the component should take a `status` prop ('waiting', 'approved', 'rejected', 'completed'). For the Badge, create a Storybook story that displays all status variants to confirm correct color mapping and styling. Unit test the Badge to ensure the `status` prop correctly maps to the theme color.

subtasks.title: Create Card.js Component File and Basic Structure
subtasks.description: Initialize the `Card.js` file within `src/components/`. Set up a basic React Native functional component that accepts and renders `children` props within a `View`.
subtasks.details: Create the file at `src/components/Card.js`. Example: `const Card = ({ children, style }) => <View style={[styles.container, style]}>{children}</View>;`
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify the file is created and the component can render simple text passed as a child element without crashing.

subtasks.title: Apply Theme-Based Styling to the Card Component
subtasks.description: Enhance the `Card` component by applying styles for background color, border radius, padding, and shadow. These styles must be derived from the application's theme.
subtasks.details: Access the theme context to retrieve styling values. Apply a background color (e.g., `theme.colors.surface`), padding (e.g., `theme.spacing.m`), and border radius (e.g., `theme.radii.m`). Implement platform-specific shadow for iOS and elevation for Android.
subtasks.testStrategy: Visually test the component on a screen with a different background color to confirm shadow and padding are correctly applied. Render various child elements inside to test content layout.

subtasks.title: Create Badge.js Component File and Define Prop Interface
subtasks.description: Create the `src/components/Badge.js` file. Set up a functional component that accepts a `status` prop with defined possible values ('waiting', 'approved', 'rejected', 'completed') and renders a `View` containing a `Text` element.
subtasks.details: Create the file `src/components/Badge.js`. The component signature should be `const Badge = ({ status }) => { ... };`. It should be prepared to handle dynamic styling and text content based on the `status` prop.
subtasks.testStrategy: Confirm the file is created and the component renders a default state without errors when passed a valid status prop.

subtasks.title: Implement Dynamic Styling and Text Mapping for Badge
subtasks.description: Implement the core logic for the `Badge` component. This includes mapping the `status` prop to a specific background color from the theme and a corresponding Korean text label (e.g., 'waiting' -> '대기중').
subtasks.details: Create a helper function or a configuration object to map each status to its theme color and text. For example: `const config = { waiting: { color: theme.colors.warning, text: '대기중' }, approved: { color: theme.colors.success, text: '승인' } };`. Use this config to dynamically set the `backgroundColor` of the `View` and the content of the `Text` component.

subtasks.title: Finalize Badge Styling and Document with Storybook
subtasks.description: Add final styling touches to the Badge, such as padding, border radius, and text styling. Create a Storybook story to display all variants of the Badge, and an example of the Card containing content.

Create `Badge.stories.js` to render a list of all badge variants ('waiting', 'approved', 'rejected', 'completed') for visual regression testing.

8. Additionally, confirm that data is still fetched and displayed correctly on these screens when a user is logged in, ensuring the listeners still function as intended.

tasks.title: Create `AdminOwnedVehicleDetailScreen`
tasks.description: Build a new screen to show detailed information about an admin-owned vehicle and allow the admin to mark it as sold.
tasks.details: Create a new screen component `AdminOwnedVehicleDetailScreen`. This screen receives an `vehicleId` as a navigation parameter. It will fetch and display all data for that vehicle from the `admin_owned_vehicles` collection. Include a button '[판매완료 처리]'. Tapping this button will open a modal to input the `soldPrice`. On confirmation, update the vehicle's document in Firestore, setting `status` to 'sold', and adding `soldPrice` and `soldDate`.

Check Firestore to confirm the document's status and sold fields are updated. After selling, confirm the vehicle is no longer visible in the `OwnedVehiclesList` on `AdminPageScreen`.

Use a `useEffect` hook to fetch the document from `firestore().collection('admin_owned_vehicles').doc(vehicleId)`. Manage loading and error states. Render the vehicle's data using appropriate components like `Text` and `View` within a `ScrollView`.

subtasks.title: Implement Firestore Update Logic for Selling Vehicle
subtasks.description: Develop the function that executes when the admin confirms the sale in the modal. This function will update the corresponding vehicle document in Firestore with the new status, sold price, and sold date.
subtasks.details: Create an asynchronous function that will be called by the modal's 'Confirm' button. This function should perform a `firestore().collection('admin_owned_vehicles').doc(vehicleId).update()` operation. The data to update is `{ status: 'sold', soldPrice: <price_from_input>, soldDate: firestore.FieldValue.serverTimestamp() }`.

subtasks.description: After successfully updating the vehicle's status to 'sold' in Firestore, provide feedback to the user and navigate them away from the detail screen.
subtasks.details: Upon a successful Firestore update, close the modal, display a success message to the admin (e.g., using a toast or an alert), and then use the `navigation.goBack()` method to return the user to the previous screen (the vehicle list). Implement error handling for the update operation.

tasks.title: Update Firebase Security Rules
tasks.description: Update and deploy Firebase Security Rules to secure the modified `consultation_requests` collection and the new `admin_owned_vehicles` collection.
tasks.details: Open the `firestore.rules` file. Update the rule for `/consultation_requests/{docId}` to reflect the logic in the PRD, allowing admins to write and users to update their own requests under specific conditions. Add a new rule block for `/admin_owned_vehicles/{docId}` that restricts all read and write access to authenticated users with an 'admin' role (`request.auth.token.role == 'admin'`).
tasks.testStrategy: Use the Firestore Rules Playground in the Firebase Console. Simulate various scenarios: 1. An unauthenticated user trying to read/write. 2. A non-admin user trying to read/write `admin_owned_vehicles`. 3. An admin user successfully reading/writing both collections. 4. A non-admin user trying to update another user's consultation request. All tests should pass or fail as expected.

subtasks.title: Analyze Existing Rules and New Schemas
subtasks.description: Review the current `firestore.rules` file to understand the existing security structure. Cross-reference the updated schema for `consultation_requests` and the new schema for `admin_owned_vehicles` from Task 33 to prepare for the rule implementation.
subtasks.details: Locate the `firestore.rules` file in the project. Read the existing rules for `users`, `vehicles`, and `consultation_requests` to understand current patterns and any helper functions. This will ensure the new rules are consistent with the existing structure.

subtasks.title: Implement Security Rules for `admin_owned_vehicles`
subtasks.description: Add a new rule block in `firestore.rules` for the `admin_owned_vehicles` collection. This rule must restrict all read and write operations to authenticated users with a custom claim of `role == 'admin'`.
subtasks.details: In `firestore.rules`, add a new match block: `match /admin_owned_vehicles/{vehicleId} { allow read, write: if request.auth.token.role == 'admin'; }`. This ensures that no other user type can access this sensitive data.
subtasks.testStrategy: Use the Firebase Rules Playground to simulate a non-admin authenticated user and an unauthenticated user attempting to read/write to `/admin_owned_vehicles/someId`. Both attempts should be denied. Simulate an admin user, which should be allowed.

subtasks.title: Update Security Rules for `consultation_requests`
subtasks.description: Modify the existing security rules for the `/consultation_requests/{docId}` path to align with the new logic. Admins should have full write access, while users can only update their own requests under specific conditions.
subtasks.details: Locate the `match /consultation_requests/{docId}` block. Update the `allow write` rule to be a combination of conditions: `(request.auth.token.role == 'admin') || (request.auth.uid == resource.data.userId && /* add other conditions from PRD */)`. Ensure the `create` rule still allows users to create their own requests.
subtasks.testStrategy: Using the Rules Playground, test the following scenarios: 1. An admin can update any field. 2. A user can update a field on their own request. 3. A user is blocked from updating a request owned by another user. 4. A user is blocked from updating a request if its status is 'completed'.

subtasks.title: Execute Local Testing via Emulator Suite
subtasks.description: Using the Firebase Emulator Suite and the project's testing framework, write and execute unit tests for the newly added and updated security rules. This ensures all access paths are explicitly tested before deployment.
subtasks.details: In the existing security rules test file (e.g., `firestore.rules.spec.js`), add new test suites for `admin_owned_vehicles` and `consultation_requests`. Create mock data and simulate authenticated users (admin, non-admin) and unauthenticated users attempting valid and invalid operations.
subtasks.testStrategy: Run the test script (e.g., `npm test`) and ensure all test cases pass. The test report should show coverage for all new and modified rule paths. Fix any failing tests before proceeding.

subtasks.title: Deploy `firestore.rules` and Verify in Console
subtasks.description: Deploy the updated and tested `firestore.rules` file to the live Firebase project using the Firebase CLI. After deployment, perform a final verification using the Firebase Console.
subtasks.details: From the project root directory, run the command `firebase deploy --only firestore:rules`. After the CLI reports a successful deployment, navigate to the Firestore Rules tab in the Firebase Console to confirm the new rules are visible and active.
subtasks.testStrategy: Perform a final smoke test using the Rules Playground in the live Firebase Console. Repeat one key test for each collection (e.g., admin access to `admin_owned_vehicles`, user access to their `consultation_request`) to confirm the deployed rules are working as expected in the production environment.
